citation.title: A Class of Unbiased Estimators of the Average Treatment Effect in Randomized Experiments

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population, design-based potential-outcomes setting (the Neyman-Rubin model): potential outcomes and covariates are fixed and the only randomness is the assignment of units to treatment and control. Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) Section 3, pp. 137-138 (PDF pp. 3-4): 'Define a binary treatment indicator $T_i$ for units $i = 1,2,\ldots,N$ such that $T_i = 1$ when unit $i$ receives the treatment and $T_i = 0$ otherwise. If the stable unit treatment value assumption [16] holds, let $Y_{1i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is exposed to the treatment, and let $Y_{0i}$ be the potential outcome if unit $i$ is not exposed to the treatment. The observed outcome $Y_i$ may be expressed as a function of the potential outcomes and the treatment: $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. [1] The causal effect of the treatment on unit $i$, $\tau_i$, is defined as the difference between the two potential outcomes for unit $i$: $\tau_i \equiv Y_{1i} - Y_{0i}$. [2] The ATE, denoted by $\Delta$, is defined as the average value of $\tau_i$ for all units $i$. In the Neyman-Rubin model, the only random component is the allocation of units to treatment and control groups.' Eq. [3]: $\Delta = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i}{N} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Y_{1i}-Y_{0i})}{N} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right]$, 'where $Y_1^T$ is the sum of the potential outcomes if in the treatment condition and $Y_0^T$ is the sum of potential outcomes if in the control condition.' Eq. [4]: $\widehat{\Delta} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y_1^T} - \widehat{Y_0^T}\right]$, 'where $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ is the estimated sum of potential outcomes under treatment and $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ is the estimated sum of potential outcomes under control.' Footnote 2 (p. 138): 'This assumption is made without loss of generality; multiple discrete treatments (or equivalently, some units not being sampled into either treatment or control) are easily accommodated in this framework. All instances of $(1 - T_i)$ in the text may be replaced by $C_i$, an indicator variable for whether or not unit $i$ receives the control, with one exception to be noted in Section 6.'

(S2) p. 138 (PDF p. 4): 'Formally, the bias of an estimator is the difference between the expected value of the estimator and the true parameter of interest; an estimator is unbiased if this difference is equal to zero. If the estimators $\widehat{Y_0^T}$ and $\widehat{Y_1^T}$ are unbiased, the corresponding estimator of $\Delta$ is also unbiased since $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_1^T}] - \mathrm{E}[\widehat{Y_0^T}]\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[Y_1^T - Y_0^T\right] = \Delta$.' [5]

(S3) Section 4, p. 138 (PDF p. 4): 'Define $N$ as the number of units in the study, $\pi_{1i}$ as the probability that unit $i$ is selected into treatment, and $\pi_{0i}$ as the probability that unit $i$ is selected into control. We assume that, $\forall i$, $\pi_{1i} > 0$ and $\pi_{0i} > 0$, or that there is a nonzero probability that each unit will be selected into treatment and that there is a nonzero probability that each unit will be selected into control. (When all units are assigned to either treatment or control, $\pi_{0i} + \pi_{1i} = 1$.)'

(S4) Section 5, pp. 140-141 (PDF pp. 6-7): eqs. [13]-[14], $\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$ and $\widehat{Y_0^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-T_i)\frac{Y_{0i}}{\pi_{0i}} - (1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$, 'where $f(.)$ is a predetermined real-valued function of pretreatment covariate vector $\mathbf{X_i}$ and of parameter vector $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$'; eq. [15], $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} - \widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right)$; eq. [16], $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$.

(S5) Section 6.1, p. 143 (PDF p. 9): '$\pi_{1i1j}$ is the probability that units $i$ and $j$ are jointly included in the treatment group'; '$\pi_{0i0j}$ is the probability that units $i$ and $j$ are jointly included in the control group'; '$\pi_{1i0j}$ is the joint probability that unit $i$ will be in the treatment group and unit $j$ will be in the control group.'

(S6) Section 6.2, pp. 143-144 (PDF pp. 9-10): 'When $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ is constant, we may simply redefine the outcome variable, $U_i = Y_i - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$. It follows that $U_{0i} = Y_{0i} - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ and $U_{1i} = Y_{1i} - f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$.' and 'As we proceed, for notational clarity, we use $Y_i$ as the outcome measure, noting that the variances derived will also apply to the generalized difference estimator if $U_i$ is substituted for $Y_i$ (along with both associated potential outcomes) and $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ is constant.'

(S7) Section 6.3, pp. 144-145 (PDF pp. 10-11), cluster totals: 'Note that if, for some units $i,j$, $\Pr(T_i \neq T_j) = 0$, then the total estimators may be equivalently rewritten. Define $K_k \in \mathbf{K}$ as the set of unit indices $i$ that satisfy $T_i = T'_k$, where $T'_k$ is indexed over all $|\mathbf{K}|$ unique random variables in $\{T_i : i = (1,2,\ldots,N)\}$. Define $\pi'_{1k}$ as the value of $\pi_{1i}, \forall i \in K_k$, $\pi'_{0k}$ as the value of $\pi_{0i}, \forall i \in K_k$. Joint probabilities $\pi'_{1k1l}$, $\pi'_{1k0l}$, and $\pi'_{0k0l}$ are defined analogously.' With '$Y'_k = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_i$' (p. 144) and '$Y'_{1k} = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_{1i}$ and $Y'_{0k} = \sum_{i \in K_k} Y_{0i}$' (p. 145). The sums over clusters run over $k = 1,\ldots,M$.

(S8) Section 6.4, p. 145 (PDF p. 11): 'Our goal is now to derive conservative variance estimators: although not unbiased, these estimators are guaranteed to have a nonnegative bias.' Footnote 7: 'Although the variance estimator is nonnegatively biased, the associated standard errors may not be (due to Jensen's inequality) and any particular draw may be above or below the true value of the variance due to sampling variability.'

Reading conventions used in every target below (they follow from (S1)-(S7) in the two-arm case that the paper works in; stated here for the formalizer and flagged as conventions, not quotations): the assignment vector $(T_1,\ldots,T_N)$ has an arbitrary probability distribution on $\{0,1\}^N$ (a finite sample space), and all expectations, variances and covariances are taken over it; every unit is assigned to treatment or control, so $\pi_{1i} = \Pr(T_i = 1)$, $\pi_{0i} = \Pr(T_i = 0) = 1 - \pi_{1i}$, $\pi_{1i1j} = \Pr(T_i = 1, T_j = 1)$, $\pi_{0i0j} = \Pr(T_i = 0, T_j = 0)$, $\pi_{1i0j} = \Pr(T_i = 1, T_j = 0)$, hence $\pi_{1i1i} = \pi_{1i}$, $\pi_{0i0i} = \pi_{0i}$ and $\pi_{1i0i} = 0$, and likewise for the primed cluster quantities; the clusters $K_1,\ldots,K_M$ partition $\{1,\ldots,N\}$, $T_i = T'_k$ for every $i \in K_k$, and distinct clusters have distinct indicators, $\Pr(T'_k \neq T'_l) > 0$ for $k \neq l$; every double sum over $k, l$ (or $i, j$) is over ordered pairs; 'the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever' means $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$ for every unit $i$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Eq. [17] with the expectation bracket closed after the third sum, with eqs. [18] and [19] (bias of the generalized difference estimator when f(X_i, theta_i) depends on the randomization)
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). Generalized difference estimator: eqs. [13]-[14], p. 140 (PDF p. 6), $\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$ and $\widehat{Y_0^{T*}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[(1-T_i)\frac{Y_{0i}}{\pi_{0i}} - (1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}} + f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})\right]$, 'where $f(.)$ is a predetermined real-valued function of pretreatment covariate vector $\mathbf{X_i}$ and of parameter vector $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$'; eq. [15], p. 141 (PDF p. 7), $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \frac{1}{N}\left(\widehat{Y_1^{T*}} - \widehat{Y_0^{T*}}\right)$; eq. [16], p. 141, $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$. Eq. [17] as printed (p. 141), with the bracket opened after the second $\mathrm{E}$ never closed: $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{Y_1^{T*}}\right] = \mathrm{E}\Big[\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{Y_{1i}}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} + \sum_{i=1}^{N}f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}) = Y_1^T - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Cov}\left(T_i,\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}}\right)$. Text before it: 'If $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ is derived from the data, unbiasedness is not guaranteed because the value of $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ can depend on the particular randomization, and thus $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}))$ is not generally equal to zero. Formally, the estimator will generally be biased because'.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P026-N001 (Sol's smallest_repair gives eq. [17] with the bracket closed after the third sum). The identity uses only $\mathrm{E}[T_i] = \pi_{1i}$, $\mathrm{E}[1 - T_i] = \pi_{0i}$ and fixed potential outcomes: $\mathrm{E}[T_i f_i/\pi_{1i}] = \mathrm{Cov}(T_i, f_i/\pi_{1i}) + \mathrm{E}[f_i]$. In the two-arm case eq. [19] equals $-\frac{1}{N}\sum_i \mathrm{Cov}(T_i, f_i)\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}} + \frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Table 2, column G (Logit) (rows SE, RMSE, Var, E[Var-hat], SE, RMSE), corrected for the population printed in Table 1
canonical_claim.location: Table 2, p. 149 (PDF p. 15); Table 1, p. 147 (PDF p. 13); Section 7.1, p. 148 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
Printed: Table 2, column G (Logit): $\Delta = 0.000$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}] = 0.000$; Bias $= 0.000$; SE $= 0.170$; RMSE $= 0.170$; Var $= 0.029$; $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}] = 0.029$; Bias $= 0.000$; SE $= 0.007$; RMSE $= 0.007$.

Corrected statement (Table 1 and Section 7.1 kept as printed). Let $\sigma(z) = 1 - 1/(1 + \exp(z))$. For a block $b'$ let $\ell_{b'}(\beta_0,\beta_1) = \sum_{i \text{ in block } b'}\left[Y_i\log\sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_i) + (1 - Y_i)\log(1 - \sigma(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_i))\right]$ be the logistic log-likelihood of the units of that block (data of Table 1).
(a) Each of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ has a unique maximizer in $\mathbb{R}^2$ (the printed data are not separated: in block 1 the outcomes at $X = 0$ and $X = 4$ are $1$ and the outcome at $X = 2$ is $0$; in block 2 outcomes at $X = 1$ and $X = 4$ are $1$ and an outcome at $X = 2$ is $0$). The maximizer of $\ell_2$, used for units in block 1, is $(\beta_{01},\beta_{11}) \approx (-1.1201076, 0.5657586)$; the maximizer of $\ell_1$, used for units in block 2, is $(\beta_{02},\beta_{12}) \approx (1.0843223, 0.2280259)$.
(b) With $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}) = \sigma(\beta_{0b} + \beta_{1b}X_i)$ for a unit $i$ in block $b$ and the 90 equiprobable assignments: $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta_G}] = 0$ exactly; $0.247090 \leq \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta_G})} \leq 0.247093$; $0.0605 \leq \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta_G}) < 0.0615$ ($\approx 0.0610543$); $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_G)] = \mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta_G})$ exactly; and the standard deviation of $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_G)$ lies in $[0.0125, 0.0135)$ ($\approx 0.0125667$).
(c) So the column reads, in the row order of Table 2, $0.000$; $0.000$; $0.000$; $0.247$; $0.247$; $0.061$; $0.061$; $0.000$; $0.013$; $0.013$, and the six printed entries $0.170$, $0.170$, $0.029$, $0.029$, $0.007$, $0.007$ are false for the printed population (for instance the interval in (b) for the SE is disjoint from $[0.1695, 0.1705)$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The population of Table 1, the design (90 equiprobable assignments), the row definitions of Table 2, the specifications of Section 7.1 and the estimators (eq. [16], and eq. [35] applied to the cluster totals of $U_i$ with $N = 16$, $M = 10$): as transcribed in the definitions of P026-T6. Logistic form, p. 141 (PDF p. 7): 'if the relationship were thought to follow a logistic function (for binary $Y_i$), $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}) = 1 - 1/(1 + \exp(\theta_{\mathbf{i}}'\mathbf{X_i}))$.' 'A logistic regression' is read as unpenalized maximum likelihood with an intercept and $X$.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P026-N003 is rated Minor because what it establishes is the G (Logit) column of the Table 1 / Table 2 inconsistency, the same defect as P026-E003 (P026-T6, P026-T7); its separate allegation (separated fits) is not established for the printed data and is not a target. From Sol's smallest_repair ('replace six G (Logit) entries: SE/RMSE(ATE) 0.170 -> 0.247; Var/E(Vhat) 0.029 -> 0.061; SE/RMSE(Vhat) 0.007 -> 0.013') and sections 2, 6 and 7 of the validator's derivation, which certify the intervals by exact rational enclosures of the two maximizers (radius $10^{-10}$ around rational odds approximations). The quantities are not rational, so the target is stated by intervals; existence and uniqueness of the maximizers (a) is the part most likely to need care in Lean. The point values were recomputed in floating point when this target was fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ri package, estate(): help text 'unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimation' and 'when HT=TRUE, invokes the Horvitz-Thompson (difference-in-totals) estimator', read with the documented covariate argument X; code branch '# Raj-Within' (HT == TRUE and X supplied)
canonical_claim.location: Not in the article PDF. Staged package source: packages/ri/ri/man/estate.Rd, lines 8 and 30; packages/ri/ri/R/estate.R, lines 15 and 31-36
canonical_claim.statement:
Statement refuted (package documentation, read as the validator read it: that calling estate() with HT = TRUE keeps the unbiasedness of Horvitz-Thompson estimation when covariates X are supplied). man/estate.Rd, description: 'Function for estimating the average treatment effect (ATE). Permits regression adjustment for covariates, difference estimation (with a pretreatment measure of the outcome variable), inverse probability weighting, and unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimation.' Argument HT: 'when HT=TRUE, invokes the Horvitz-Thompson (difference-in-totals) estimator. When HT=FALSE, invokes the inverse-probability-weighted regression estimator'. Argument X: 'N-by-k numeric matrix of covariates for regression adjustment'. Code (R/estate.R): 'weights <- Z/prob + (1-Z)/(1-prob)' and, under the comment '# Raj-Within', 'if (HT == TRUE & !is.null(X)) { Ypre2 <- lm(Yd~X)\$fitted; Yd2 <- Yd - Ypre2; ate <- (sum(Yd2[Z==1]*weights[Z==1]) - sum(Yd2[Z==0]*weights[Z==0]))/length(Yd) }' (line breaks of the source are shown as semicolons, and the R operator \$ is written with a backslash).

In the paper's notation the branch computes $\widehat{\Delta}_X = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{T_i}{\pi_{1i}}(Y_i - \widehat{f}_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1-T_i}{\pi_{0i}}(Y_i - \widehat{f}_i)\right]$, where $\widehat{f}_i$ is the fitted value for unit $i$ of the ordinary least squares regression of the observed outcomes $Y_1,\ldots,Y_N$ on an intercept and $X$, fitted on all $N$ units.

Counterexample (the validator's; exact arithmetic). $N = 3$; $X = (0,1,2)$; $Y_{0i} = 0$ and $Y_{1i} = 1$ for all $i$, so $\Delta = 1$; exactly one unit is treated, each with probability $1/3$, so $\pi_{1i} = 1/3$ and $\pi_{0i} = 2/3$ (complete random assignment, Section 4.1.1). When unit 1, 2 or 3 is the treated unit, the fitted values are $(5/6, 1/3, -1/6)$, $(1/3, 1/3, 1/3)$, $(-1/6, 1/3, 5/6)$ and $\widehat{\Delta}_X = 1/4$, $1$, $1/4$ respectively. Hence $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}_X] = 1/2 \neq 1 = \Delta$: the bias is $-1/2$. This agrees with the paper's eq. [19]: $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,\widehat{f}_i) = (1/6, 0, 1/6)$ for $i = 1,2,3$ and $-\frac{1}{3}\left(3 + \frac{3}{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{6} + 0 + \frac{1}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}$. With the same design and no covariate adjustment the HT estimator of eq. [8] equals $1$ on every assignment.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). HT estimator: eqs. [6]-[8], p. 139 (PDF p. 5), $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_{1i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_i$, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_i$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} - \widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}Y_iT_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}Y_i(1-T_i)\right]$. Eq. [16], p. 141 (PDF p. 7): $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$. Eq. [19], p. 142 (PDF p. 8): $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\Delta_G}\right] - \Delta = \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Cov}\left((1-T_i),\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right) - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Cov}\left(T_i,\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}}\right)\right)$. Section 5.1, p. 141: 'If $\theta_{\mathbf{i}}$ is derived from the data, unbiasedness is not guaranteed because the value of $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})$ can depend on the particular randomization, and thus $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}))$ is not generally equal to zero.' In R, lm(Yd~X) is least squares with an intercept; Z is the treatment indicator and prob the vector of $\pi_{1i}$.
canonical_claim.note: Finding P026-N004 is about the package's documentation, not a statement in the article; it is included because it rests on an exact formal counterexample and the correction qualifies an unbiasedness claim. The article itself says that fits from the data at hand are biased and its results are not contradicted (the bias here is the one eq. [19] predicts). From validate/P026-N004/v1/artifact/derivation.md; the three estimates, the fitted values and the covariances were recomputed when this target was fixed. This statement is transcribed from the staged package files, since it has no page image.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: ri package, estate(): help text for HT = TRUE, corrected (formal content of the qualified claim)
canonical_claim.location: Not in the article PDF. Staged package source: packages/ri/ri/man/estate.Rd, lines 8 and 30; packages/ri/ri/R/estate.R, lines 4-6, 15, 29 and 31-36
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected statement (formal content of the repaired help text). Under the standing assumptions, with the assignment probabilities supplied correctly:
(a) (HT = TRUE, X = NULL.) For any vector $g = (g_1,\ldots,g_N)$ fixed before randomization (the argument Ypre; $g = 0$ when it is absent), the function returns $\widehat{\Delta}_g = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{T_i}{\pi_{1i}}(Y_i - g_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1-T_i}{\pi_{0i}}(Y_i - g_i)\right]$, and $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}_g] = \Delta$.
(b) (HT = TRUE, X supplied.) The function returns $\widehat{\Delta}_X = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{T_i}{\pi_{1i}}(Y_i - \widehat{f}_i) - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1-T_i}{\pi_{0i}}(Y_i - \widehat{f}_i)\right]$ with $\widehat{f}_i$ the fitted values of the least squares regression of the observed outcomes on an intercept and $X$ over all $N$ units; this is $\widehat{\Delta_G}$ of eq. [16] with $f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}}) = \widehat{f}_i$, a function of the realized assignment, and by eq. [19] $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}_X] - \Delta = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,\widehat{f}_i)\left(\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}} + \frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$.
(c) The estimator in (b) is not unbiased in general: there is a design satisfying the standing assumptions (P026-T15) with $\mathrm{E}[\widehat{\Delta}_X] = 1/2$ and $\Delta = 1$. It is unbiased whenever $\mathrm{Cov}(T_i,\widehat{f}_i) = 0$ for all $i$, for example under the sharp null $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$ for all $i$, where the observed outcomes and hence the $\widehat{f}_i$ do not vary with the assignment.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eq. [1], p. 138 (PDF p. 4): $Y_i = T_iY_{1i} + (1-T_i)Y_{0i}$. ATE, eq. [3], p. 138: $\Delta = \frac{1}{N}[Y_1^T - Y_0^T]$ with $Y_1^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{1i}$, $Y_0^T = \sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_{0i}$. Probabilities $\pi_{1i} > 0$, $\pi_{0i} > 0$: Section 4, p. 138, quoted in standing assumption (S3). HT estimator: eqs. [6]-[8], p. 139 (PDF p. 5), $\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_{1i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}T_iY_i$, $\widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_{0i} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}(1-T_i)Y_i$, $\widehat{\Delta_{HT}} = \frac{1}{N}\left[\widehat{Y^T_{1,HT}} - \widehat{Y^T_{0,HT}}\right] = \frac{1}{N}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{1i}}Y_iT_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{\pi_{0i}}Y_i(1-T_i)\right]$. Eq. [16], p. 141 (PDF p. 7): $\widehat{\Delta_G} = \widehat{\Delta_{HT}} - \frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_i\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{1i}} - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(1-T_i)\frac{f(\mathbf{X_i},\theta_{\mathbf{i}})}{\pi_{0i}}\right)$. Eq. canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. (i) p. 145 (PDF p. 11), between eqs. [29] and [30]: 'The covariance expression in eq. [29] may now be simplified, however. Since, for all pairs $k,l$ such that $k 
eq l$, $\Pr(T'_k 
eq T'_l) > 0$, then $\pi'_{1k0l} > 0$ for all $l 
eq k$. Therefore, the covariance expression may be reduced further.' Footnote 6 (attached to that sentence): 'If there are multiple treatments, the following simplification cannot be used. Furthermore, the associated estimator in Section 6.4 must apply to eq. [29], for which the derivation is trivially different.'
(ii) p. 146 (PDF p. 12): 'However, again using Young's inequality, we can derive a generally conservative (which is, in this case, nonpositively biased) covariance estimator: $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C\left(\widehat{Y_1^T},\widehat{Y_0^T}ight) = \sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{l
eq k} rac{T'_k(1-T'_l)}{\pi'_{1k0l}}(\pi'_{1k0l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}) rac{Y'_kY'_l}{\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}} - \sum_{k=1}^{M}T'_k rac{(Y'_k)^2}{2\pi'_{1k}} - \sum_{k=1}^{M}(1-T'_k) rac{(Y'_k)^2}{2\pi'_{0k}}$. [34] In Appendix E, we prove that $\mathrm{E}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C\left(\widehat{Y_1^T},\widehat{Y_0^T}ight)ight] \leq \mathrm{Cov}\left(\widehat{Y_1^T},\widehat{Y_0^T}ight)$. One important property of this estimator is that, under the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect whatsoever, this estimator is unbiased.'
(iii) p. 147 (PDF p. 13): 'Combining and simplifying eqs. [32], [33], and [34], we can construct a conservative estimator of $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_{HT})$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_{HT}) =  rac{1}{N^2}\sum_{k=1}^{M}\Bigg[T'_k\left( rac{Y'_k}{\pi'_{1k}}ight)^2 + (1-T'_k)\left( rac{Y'_k}{\pi'_{0k}}ight)^2 + \sum_{l
eq k}\Bigg( rac{T'_kT'_l}{\pi'_{1k1l}+\varepsilon_{1k1l}}(\pi'_{1k1l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{1l}) rac{Y'_k}{\pi'_{1k}} rac{Y'_l}{\pi'_{1l}} +  rac{(1-T'_k)(1-T'_l)}{\pi'_{0k0l}+\varepsilon_{0k0l}}(\pi'_{0k0l}-\pi'_{0k}\pi'_{0l}) rac{Y'_k}{\pi'_{0k}} rac{Y'_l}{\pi'_{0l}} - 2 rac{T'_k(1-T'_l)}{\pi'_{1k0l}+\varepsilon_{1k0l}}(\pi'_{1k0l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}) rac{Y'_kY'_l}{\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}}\Bigg) + \sum_{ orall l:\pi'_{1k1l}=0}\left(T'_k rac{(Y'_k)^2}{2\pi'_{1k}} + T'_l rac{(Y'_l)^2}{2\pi'_{1l}}ight) + \sum_{ orall l:\pi'_{0k0l}=0}\left((1-T'_k) rac{(Y'_k)^2}{2\pi'_{0k}} + (1-T'_l) rac{(Y'_l)^2}{2\pi'_{0l}}ight)\Bigg]$, [35] where $\varepsilon_{akbl} = 1[\pi'_{akbl} = 0]$. ($\varepsilon_{akbl}$ is included to avoid division by zero.) The fact that $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_{HT})$ is conservative has been established. But also note that when, for all $k,l$, $\pi'_{1k1l} > 0$ and $\pi'_{0k0l} > 0$, and there is no treatment effect whatsoever, the estimator is exactly unbiased. A proof of this statement trivially follows from the fact that when $Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$, eq. [1] reduces to $Y_i = Y_{1i} = Y_{0i}$, which is not a random variable.'
(iv) Footnote 9 (p. 147): '$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_G)$, the variance estimator as applied to $U_i$, is not generally guaranteed to be conservative. Specifically, when $f(\mathbf{X_i},	heta_{\mathbf{i}})$ not constant, there is no guarantee that $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_G)$ will be conservative, though an analogy to linearized estimators suggests that it should be approximately conservative with large $N$. Importantly, however, when, for all $k,l$, $\pi'_{1k1l} > 0$ and $\pi'_{0k0l} > 0$ and the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect holds, $\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_C(\widehat{\Delta}_G)$ is unbiased for $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\Delta}_G)$.'
(v) p. 137 (PDF p. 3): 'Our article extends this prior work by proposing a new Horvitz-Thompson-based variance estimator that is conservative for any experimental design, though additional regularity conditions would be required for use in constructing confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.' Abstract (p. 135): 'We then provide expressions and conservative estimators for the variance of the proposed estimators.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Cluster notation and the cluster-level HT totals $\widehat{Y_1^T}$, $\widehat{Y_0^T}$: standing assumption (S7) and the definitions of P026-T1. Eqs. [32] and [33]: transcribed in the definitions of P026-T2. Eq. [30], p. 145 (PDF p. 11): $\mathrm{Cov}\left(\widehat{Y_1^T},\widehat{Y_0^T}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{l\neq k}(\pi'_{1k0l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l})\frac{Y'_{1k}Y'_{0l}}{\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}} - \sum_{k=1}^{M}Y'_{1k}Y'_{0k}$. Eq. [29], p. 145 (PDF p. 11): $\mathrm{Cov}\left(\widehat{Y_1^T},\widehat{Y_0^T}\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{l=1}^{M}(\pi'_{1k0l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l})\frac{Y'_{1k}Y'_{0l}}{\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}} = \sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{\forall l:\pi'_{1k0l}\neq 0}(\pi'_{1k0l}-\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l})\frac{Y'_{1k}Y'_{0l}}{\pi'_{1k}\pi'_{0l}} - \sum_{k=1}^{M}\sum_{\forall l:\pi'_{1k0l}=0}Y'_{1k}Y'_{0l}$. Conservative means nonnegatively biased (standing assumption (S8)); for the covariance estimator the paper says 'conservative (which is, in this case, nonpositively biased)'. In (iii), 'for all $k,l$' includes $k = l$, where $\pi'_{1k1k} = \pi'_{1k}$ and $\pi'_{0k0k} = \pi'_{0k}$ are positive by assumption.
